lesson.menu_desc: What happens if, and what always happens when -- first and zero conditional
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- If the Cue Runs Long
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 7 -- If the Cue Runs Long

listenings.text: Everybody who has done live television has the same conversation on their first week, and it goes like this. Somebody senior tells you that nothing ever goes exactly to plan, and you nod, and you think you understand, and you do not. Here is what it actually means. In a recorded session, a mistake is a delay. In a live show, a mistake is a decision, and you have about four seconds to make it. So the preparation is not about preventing problems, because you cannot. It is about deciding, calmly, in a quiet room, three days earlier, what you will do when each of them happens. If the backing track drops out, who speaks first? If the singer starts in the wrong key, do we let it run or do we abort? If the cue runs long, does the picture cut or does the music fade? Write the answers down. Nobody thinks clearly at nine on a Sunday night, and the version of you that is sitting here now is much smarter than the version of you that will be standing there.

The most useful thing anybody ever taught me was a habit, not a technique, and it takes about ninety seconds. Before every live show I sit down and I write three lines. What is the single most likely thing to go wrong tonight, what will I do in the first four seconds if it does, and who needs to know before I do it. That is it. Three lines. And the strange part is that the answer to the first question is almost never the dramatic one. It is never the power. It is never the building. It is a laptop that has decided to install something, or a musician who changed a key on Friday and told one person. I have done this before every show for six years, and the thing I wrote down has actually happened maybe eleven times. That is a terrible success rate for a prediction and a fantastic one for a habit, because the eleven times it happened, nobody in the room saw me think. They just saw me move.

extra_audio.text: Pedro starts with the rule that never changes: if a track drops out, the room goes quiet. Then he names the most likely problem of the night. He says that if the cue runs long, the picture will cut and the music will fade under it. He explains that if the singer starts in the wrong key, they will let it run and fix it after the break. He adds that there is a backup on a second machine, and that he will patch it in four seconds. Then he asks the other person who needs to know before anything changes.
